explain.say: Imagine you walk into the kitchen and see crumbs on your brother's face and an empty biscuit tin. Nobody told you, but you know who ate them! That is inference. Look at the board: a story says Amara's coat is dripping. But why?

explain.say: See the first clue? Her umbrella is leaning wet by the door. A clue is a little piece of evidence the writer leaves for you. What does a wet umbrella make you think?

explain.say: Brilliant detective work! The secret is: clue plus what I know equals my idea. Always point to the clue that proves it. Challenge: Leo hugged his gift and could not stop grinning. How does Leo feel, and which words told you?

faq.a: Inference means working out something the writer does not say directly, using clues in the text and what you already know.

faq.q: What is a clue in reading?
faq.a: A clue is a detail the writer gives you, like a wet umbrella or a shaky voice, that helps you work out something hidden.
asks: How do I find clues in a text?

faq.q: How do I make an inference?
faq.a: Find a clue, think about what you already know, then decide what it suggests. Then say: I think this because the text says...

faq.q: What is the difference between inference and guessing?
faq.a: A guess has no proof. An inference is backed up by clues in the text, so you can point to the words that support it.

faq.q: What is the difference between retrieval and inference?
faq.a: Retrieval means finding an answer written right there in the text. Inference means working out an answer that is only hinted at.
asks: Find it or work it out?

facts: Readers make inferences all the time, often without noticing, to understand feelings and reasons.
Fictional detectives like Sherlock Holmes are famous for inferring from tiny clues.
